title: Preparing an Intent-Classification Dataset
text:
Can we prepare a balanced dataset that teaches a model to route music-service messages to the correct part of the application?
Data preparation is the foundation of fine-tuning. A model can only learn the categories, boundaries, and mistakes represented in its training examples. Duplicate leakage, inconsistent labels, weak category definitions, or unrepresentative messages can make evaluation misleading and produce an unreliable classifier. For that reason, data preparation has its own notebook, where the dataset can be inspected and validated before any training begins.
The classifier needs to distinguish six intents: recommendation requests, recommendation-explanation requests, customer support, partnerships, junk, and messages that need human review. An explanation request can be sent to the RAG workflow built in the previous notebook, while the other categories follow their own routes.

title: Preparing an Intent-Classification Dataset
text:
Hypothesis
If we define one source file per intent, remove exact duplicates before splitting, and split every intent separately, the resulting training, validation, and test sets should contain all six categories without exact-message leakage between splits.
Formatting the examples with Qwen’s chat template should then produce training records containing the expected answer and test records that keep the answer separate for evaluation.

title: Preparing an Intent-Classification Dataset
text:
Environment Setup
Create or activate the project environment and install the Python dependencies before running the notebook:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
Select the .venv kernel in Jupyter. Install Ollama separately, then pull the corresponding quantized Ollama build of the instruction-tuned Qwen model used by the classification experiment:
ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b-instruct
The Ollama tag is a Q4_K_M build of the same model family; it is not numerically identical to the Hugging Face checkpoint. Ollama will run the prompting baseline and, after fine-tuning, the imported model. This preparation notebook still uses AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct") to produce Qwen-compatible training text. The first tokenizer load may download files from Hugging Face unless they are already cached.
Ollama runs models but does not perform the fine-tuning step. A training framework will create the fine-tuned weights or adapter, which can then be imported into Ollama. This notebook only prepares and formats data, so it does not require model-training hardware.

title: Preparing an Intent-Classification Dataset
text:
Experiment
We will load twelve example messages for each intent, normalize them for duplicate detection, and assign numeric labels from the order of source_files. Each intent is shuffled with a fixed random seed and split approximately 80%/10%/10%.
After saving the labelled data, we will format the training and validation examples as complete conversations. Test prompts omit the assistant answer so a later notebook can compare the model’s prediction with the stored label.

Build the labelled dataset
The first code cell performs the main data-quality work. It accepts execution from either the repository root or the notebook directory, checks every CSV for a text column and non-empty messages, and rejects identical messages assigned to conflicting labels.
casefold() and whitespace normalization make duplicate comparison insensitive to capitalization and repeated spaces. The original message text is preserved in the saved dataset. ClassLabel stores the category names with the numeric labels so later notebooks do not have to reproduce the list order. utf-8-sig accepts ordinary UTF-8 CSVs as well as files containing a byte-order mark.

import csv
import random
from pathlib import Path

from datasets import ClassLabel, Dataset, DatasetDict, Features, Value, load_from_disk

notebook_dir = Path.cwd()
if not (notebook_dir / "intentData").is_dir():
    notebook_dir = notebook_dir / "embeddings-and-search"

data_dir = notebook_dir / "data"
label_names = [
    "Recommendation_Request",
    "Explanation_Request",
    "Customer_Support",
    "Partnership",
    "Junk",
    "Human_Review",
]
source_files = [
    "recommendation_request.csv",
    "explanation_request.csv",
    "customer_support.csv",
    "partnership.csv",
    "junk.csv",
    "human_review.csv",
]

rng = random.Random(42)
split_records = {"train": [], "validation": [], "test": []}
seen = {}

for label, filename in enumerate(source_files):
    records = []
    with (notebook_dir / "intentData" / filename).open(
        newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig"
    ) as file:
        reader = csv.DictReader(file)
        if not reader.fieldnames or "text" not in reader.fieldnames:
            raise ValueError(f"{filename} must contain a text column")
        # DictReader already consumes the header.
        for row in reader:
            text = row["text"].strip()
            if not text:
                raise ValueError(f"Empty message in {filename}")
            key = " ".join(text.casefold().split())
            if key in seen:
                if seen[key] != label:
                    raise ValueError("The same message has conflicting category labels")
                continue
            seen[key] = label
            # File order defines numeric labels consistently across all splits.
            records.append({"text": text, "label": label})

    if len(records) < 10:
        raise ValueError(f"{filename} needs at least 10 unique messages")
    rng.shuffle(records)
    train_end = int(len(records) * 0.8)
    validation_end = train_end + int(len(records) * 0.1)
    split_records["train"].extend(records[:train_end])
    split_records["validation"].extend(records[train_end:validation_end])
    split_records["test"].extend(records[validation_end:])

for records in split_records.values():
    rng.shuffle(records)

dataset_features = Features({
    "text": Value("string"),
    "label": ClassLabel(names=label_names),
})
dataset = DatasetDict({
    name: Dataset.from_list(records, features=dataset_features)
    for name, records in split_records.items()
})
data_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
dataset.save_to_disk(str(data_dir / "music_service_intents_labeled"))
print(dataset)



Load the tokenizer and labelled data
The tokenizer supplies Qwen’s required conversation format; it does not train or run the model. Reloading the labelled dataset also checks that the first saved artifact can be read successfully.
The system instruction defines the six valid outputs and sends unclear or equally plausible messages to Human_Review.

from transformers import AutoTokenizer


model_id = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"


tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)


dataset = load_from_disk(str(data_dir / "music_service_intents_labeled"))
label_names = dataset["train"].features["label"].names


dataset


message_system = """
You route messages sent to a music service.
Classify each message as Recommendation_Request, Explanation_Request, Customer_Support, Partnership, Junk, or Human_Review.
Use Human_Review when the intent is unclear or more than one route is equally plausible.
Return only the category name, without an explanation.
""".strip()



Format the training and validation examples
Each record becomes a three-message conversation: a system instruction, the user’s message, and the correct category as the assistant response. Including the answer is appropriate here because these splits are used for learning and validation during training.

def convert_to_training_messages(dataset):
 messages = [
   [
    {
        "role": "system", 
        "content": message_system
    },
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": f"Classify: {ds['text']}"
    },
    {
        "role": "assistant",
        "content": label_names[ds["label"]]
    }
   ] for ds in dataset
 ]
 texts = [
  tokenizer.apply_chat_template(message, tokenize=False) 
    for message in messages
 ]
 return {"text": texts}


ds_train = convert_to_training_messages(dataset["train"])
ds_val = convert_to_training_messages(dataset["validation"])



Format the test examples
Test prompts include the system and user messages but omit the assistant answer. add_generation_prompt=True marks the point where Qwen should generate its prediction.
The numeric label remains in a separate column so evaluation code can compare the prediction with the expected category without exposing that answer in the prompt.

def convert_to_prompting_messages(dataset):
  texts = []
  labels = []
  for ds in dataset:
    message = [
      {
        "role": "system", 
        "content": message_system
      },
      {
          "role": "user",
          "content": f"Classify: {ds['text']}"
      }
    ]
    chat_message = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
      message,
      tokenize=False,
      add_generation_prompt=True,
    )
    texts.append(chat_message)
    labels.append(ds["label"])
  return {"text": texts, "label": labels}


ds_test = convert_to_prompting_messages(dataset["test"])



Assemble and save the Qwen dataset
Convert the formatted dictionaries back into Hugging Face datasets, combine the three splits, and save the result. Training and validation contain formatted text; test contains formatted text plus a separate named ClassLabel.

ds_train = Dataset.from_dict(ds_train)
ds_val = Dataset.from_dict(ds_val)
test_features = Features({
    "text": Value("string"),
    "label": ClassLabel(names=label_names),
})
ds_test = Dataset.from_dict(ds_test, features=test_features)


ds_combined = DatasetDict({
    "train": ds_train,
    "validation": ds_val,
    "test": ds_test
})


ds_combined.save_to_disk(str(data_dir / "music_service_intents_qwen"))

title: Preparing an Intent-Classification Dataset
text:
Analysis
The preparation meets the notebook’s structural goal: each intent is represented in every split, exact normalized duplicates cannot cross split boundaries, and the fixed seed makes the result reproducible. The test schema also keeps expected labels outside the model prompt.
These checks establish dataset organization, not classifier quality. A complete evaluation still needs a prompting baseline, fine-tuning, predictions on the test set, and per-category error analysis.

title: Preparing an Intent-Classification Dataset
text:
Failure Cases
Exact duplicate detection does not catch paraphrases such as “Why was this suggested?” and “What caused this recommendation?”. Closely related paraphrases in different splits could make evaluation look better than real-world performance.
Some intents naturally overlap. A message about a recommended song failing to play could be an explanation request or customer support request. Human_Review gives the system a safe route for ambiguity, but its boundary depends on consistent labelling.
The examples are small and written for this lesson. Twelve messages per intent are enough to demonstrate the pipeline but not enough to establish dependable production behavior. Real messages may contain spelling errors, multiple requests, adversarial junk, languages not represented here, or references that require conversation history.

title: Preparing an Intent-Classification Dataset
text:
Conclusion
The notebook produces two reusable artifacts. music_service_intents_labeled preserves cleaned messages and named labels, while music_service_intents_qwen stores chat-formatted training, validation, and test data. Both artifacts persist the label names wherever a label column is present.
This preparation extends the song recommendation application with a routing dataset. It does not replace the recommender or the RAG explanation workflow; it prepares a classifier that can decide which workflow should handle a message.

title: Preparing an Intent-Classification Dataset
text:
From Data Preparation to Evaluation
The next stage asks a practical question: does fine-tuning classify these messages more reliably than prompting the original model? The prepared splits support four stages:

Establish an Ollama baseline. Load raw messages from music_service_intents_labeled["test"], construct separate system and user messages, and send them to Ollama’s chat API with qwen2.5:0.5b-instruct. Do not send the already rendered text from music_service_intents_qwen as a user message, because Ollama would apply its chat template again. Save each prediction rather than judging a few examples by eye.
Fine-tune the same model family. Train on the training split, use the validation split to monitor the run, and keep the test split completely unseen. Ollama is the local runtime; a separate training framework produces the model weights or adapter.
Run the fine-tuned model through Ollama. Export the result in a compatible model format, import it under a new Ollama model name, and quantize it to Q4_K_M to match the baseline build. Classify the same raw test messages with the same instructions and generation settings.
Compare the two approaches. Measure overall accuracy, per-category results, and the confusion matrix. Inspect every error, especially useful requests marked as junk, explanation requests sent away from the RAG workflow, and unclear messages that should have reached human review.

The comparison should use the unchanged test set for both models. If fine-tuning produces little improvement, the extra training and deployment complexity may not be justified. If it improves the important routing errors, the classifier can become the entry point to the application: Recommendation_Request goes to the recommender, Explanation_Request goes to the existing RAG explanation workflow, and the remaining labels go to their corresponding queues.

title: Can Embeddings Represent a Listener’s Musical Taste?
text:
Can embeddings represent a listener’s musical taste? A song search starts with words someone types. A recommender starts with songs someone liked and tries to find unheard songs that fit. We will test whether the titles and descriptions of liked songs give us a useful starting point.
This is a small, guided experiment. You need basic Python, but no machine learning background. For the demo, we treat three plays as likes; a real app would need a better signal of preference.

title: Can Embeddings Represent a Listener’s Musical Taste?
text:
Can embeddings represent a listener’s musical taste? A song search starts with words someone types. A recommender starts with songs someone liked and tries to find unheard songs that fit. We will test whether the titles and descriptions of liked songs give us a useful starting point.
This is a small, guided experiment. You need basic Python, but no machine learning background. For the demo, we treat three plays as likes; a real app would need a better signal of preference.

title: Can Embeddings Represent a Listener’s Musical Taste?
text:
Hypothesis
Songs whose descriptions share themes with the three liked songs should rank highly among unheard songs. We turn each song’s title and description into a list of numbers called an embedding, then average the three liked songs’ embeddings to make one search query. This average, called a centroid, is our stand-in for the listener’s taste.
This tests whether written themes help find related songs. It cannot tell us whether the listener would enjoy how those songs sound.

title: Can Embeddings Represent a Listener’s Musical Taste?
text:
Experiment
We will use:

3 liked songs from one example listener
A 24-song fictional catalog in songs.csv
The all-MiniLM-L6-v2 text embedding model
Chroma to store and search the embeddings
Cosine similarity to rank songs by the listener’s preference vector

Chroma is a vector database: it stores each song’s embedding and finds songs whose vectors are close to a query. We use it because its in-memory Python client lets this small notebook run without setting up a separate database service. MiniLM creates the embeddings; Chroma stores and searches them.
The product recommender example inspired the history, retrieval, and filtering pattern.
song title + description → embedding → Chroma
3 liked-song embeddings → average (centroid) → search → remove heard songs
To run along, install dependencies from the repository root with python -m pip install -r requirements.txt. Open this notebook in Jupyter or VS Code using that Python environment, then run its cells from top to bottom. It can load songs.csv when launched from either the repository root or embeddings-and-search. The model may download on the first run.

Load the catalog
Song is a plain Python record for one CSV row. We embed each song’s title and description; the genre stays separate for a later comparison.

import csv
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Song:
    songId: str
    title: str
    artist: str
    genre: str
    description: str

    def title_and_description(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.title} {self.description}"


song_path = Path("songs.csv")
if not song_path.exists():
    song_path = Path("embeddings-and-search") / "songs.csv"

with song_path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as song_file:
    songs = [
        Song(
            songId=row["id"],
            title=row["title"],
            artist=row["artist"],
            genre=row["genre"],
            description=row["description"],
        )
        for row in csv.DictReader(song_file)
    ]

print(f"Loaded {len(songs)} songs")
print(f"Example: {songs[0].title} ({songs[0].genre}) — {songs[0].description}")

Loaded 24 songs
Example: First Light (Pop) — A song about finding hope after heartbreak.




Embed and index the songs
MiniLM makes an embedding for each song’s text. collection.upsert stores it under the song ID. Chroma keeps this collection in memory for the current session.
Chroma’s space setting chooses how it compares embeddings:







Space
What it measures




cosine
Difference in direction, regardless of vector length


l2
Squared distance between coordinates; vector length matters


ip
Inner product (dot product); direction and vector length matter



All three use the same song embeddings but can rank them differently. We choose cosine because this experiment looks for descriptions pointing in a similar semantic direction. Cosine similarity reports closeness (higher means closer), while Chroma reports cosine distance (lower means closer): distance = 1 − similarity. For example, a similarity of 0.8 is a distance of 0.2. Both give the same ranking.

import chromadb
from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions

client = chromadb.Client()
embedding_function = embedding_functions.SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(
    model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
)
collection = client.get_or_create_collection(
    "song_recommendations_cosine",
    embedding_function=embedding_function,
    configuration={"hnsw": {"space": "cosine"}},
)
collection.upsert(
    ids=[song.songId for song in songs],
    documents=[song.title_and_description() for song in songs],
)
print(f"Indexed {collection.count()} songs")

Indexed 24 songs




Record a listener’s likes
These are ordinary application classes. ListeningHistory holds songs the person liked, and User provides a convenient way to add one.

@dataclass
class ListeningHistory:
    songs: list[Song] = field(default_factory=list)

    def add_song(self, song: Song) -> None:
        self.songs.append(song)

    def has_listened_to(self, song_id: str) -> bool:
        return any(song.songId == song_id for song in self.songs)


@dataclass
class User:
    username: str
    listening_history: ListeningHistory = field(default_factory=ListeningHistory)

    def add_listen(self, song: Song) -> None:
        self.listening_history.add_song(song)





Build the centroid and retrieve songs
The recommender fetches the three stored embeddings, averages them, queries Chroma once, removes songs already heard, and ranks the remaining candidates. Repeated plays of a song count once. zip(*embeddings) groups matching coordinates for the average; results["ids"][0] selects the results of our one Chroma query.
The default same_genre_weight=0 keeps the main experiment focused on cosine similarity. The optional genre preference is examined in Analysis. We score all 24 songs here so every unheard song can be considered. A larger catalog would retrieve a smaller candidate set first.
Why convert Chroma’s distance? Smaller cosine distances mean closer text matches. semantic_score = 1 - distance / 2 turns them into 0…1 scores where higher means closer, matching the genre score below. Dividing by 2 halves each distance, changing the possible range from 0…2 to 0…1; subtracting from 1 reverses its direction.



Chroma distance
Calculation
Semantic score




0
1 - 0 / 2
1 (closest)


0.4
1 - 0.4 / 2
0.8


2
1 - 2 / 2
0 (farthest)



The conversion keeps the same song order; it is not a probability that someone will like a song.
Why this final score? Both semantic_score and genre_match run from 0 to 1. We choose same_genre_weight as the share given to genre. Subtracting it from 1 gives the share left for semantic similarity. The two shares add to 1, so their weighted average also stays between 0 and 1.
For example, with semantic_score = 0.8, genre_match = 0.4, and same_genre_weight = 0.15, genre gets 15% and semantic similarity gets 1 - 0.15 = 0.85 (85%). The final score is 0.85 × 0.8 + 0.15 × 0.4 = 0.74. The 0.15 weight is an illustrative choice, not one learned from listener data.
How are songs sorted? ranked.append((score, distance, song)) saves one tuple for each unheard song. In the sort expression, item means one of those tuples: for (0.8, 0.6, song_B), item[0] is the score 0.8, item[1] is the distance 0.6, and item[2] is the Song object. Python checks the following values in order, moving to the next one only when the previous values tie:

-item[0] puts higher scores first. Python normally sorts smaller numbers first; negating the score reverses that order.
item[1] puts the smaller Chroma distance first when scores are equal.
item[2].songId orders songs by ID when both score and distance are equal, so ties have a consistent order.




Song
Score
Distance
Order after sorting




A
0.70
0.40
3


B
0.80
0.60
1


C
0.70
0.20
2



B comes first because it has the highest score. C and A tie on score, so C comes before A because its distance is smaller.

class SongRecommender:
    def __init__(self, songs: list[Song], collection):
        self.songs_by_id = {song.songId: song for song in songs}
        self.collection = collection

    def get_recommendations(
        self,
        listening_history: ListeningHistory,
        n_recommendations: int = 3,
        same_genre_weight: float = 0.0,
    ) -> list[Song]:
        """Rank unheard songs using the listener vector and an optional genre match."""
        if n_recommendations < 0:
            raise ValueError("n_recommendations must be nonnegative")
        if not 0 <= same_genre_weight <= 1:
            raise ValueError("same_genre_weight must be between 0 and 1")
        if not listening_history.songs or n_recommendations == 0:
            return []

        # Repeated plays do not count as separate likes in this example.
        liked_songs_by_id = {song.songId: song for song in listening_history.songs}
        liked_songs = list(liked_songs_by_id.values())
        liked_ids = set(liked_songs_by_id.keys())
        unknown_ids = liked_ids - self.songs_by_id.keys()
        if unknown_ids:
            raise ValueError(f"Songs missing from the catalog: {sorted(unknown_ids)}")

        stored = self.collection.get(ids=list(liked_ids), include=["embeddings"])
        embeddings = stored["embeddings"]
        if embeddings is None or len(embeddings) != len(liked_ids):
            raise ValueError("A liked song is missing an embedding in the collection")

        listener_vector = [
            sum(float(value) for value in dimension) / len(embeddings)
            for dimension in zip(*embeddings)
        ]
        if not listener_vector:
            raise ValueError("Stored song embeddings are empty")

        # Query the whole 24-song catalog so genre reranking sees every candidate.
        results = self.collection.query(
            query_embeddings=[listener_vector],
            n_results=self.collection.count(),
            include=["distances"],
        )
        ranked = []
        for song_id, distance in zip(results["ids"][0], results["distances"][0]):
            if listening_history.has_listened_to(song_id):
                continue
            song = self.songs_by_id[song_id]
            # Chroma cosine distance runs from 0 (closest) to 2 (farthest).
            # Divide by 2 to get 0..1, then subtract from 1 so higher means closer.
            # For example, distance 0.4 becomes 1 - 0.4 / 2 = 0.8.
            semantic_score = 1 - distance / 2
            # Share of unique liked songs with this candidate's exact genre.
            genre_match = sum(
                liked.genre == song.genre for liked in liked_songs
            ) / len(liked_songs)
            # Genre gets same_genre_weight of the score; semantic similarity
            # gets the remainder, 1 - same_genre_weight. For example, 0.15
            # for genre leaves 0.85 for semantic similarity.
            score = (
                (1 - same_genre_weight) * semantic_score
                + same_genre_weight * genre_match
            )
            ranked.append((score, distance, song))

        # Each item is (score, distance, song). Check these in order:
        # -item[0]: higher scores first (Python sorts smaller values first).
        # item[1]: smaller distances first when scores tie.
        # item[2].songId: consistent order when both values tie.
        ranked.sort(key=lambda item: (-item[0], item[1], item[2].songId))
        # Take the top entries and return only their Song objects.
        return [song for _, _, song in ranked[:n_recommendations]]

title: Can Embeddings Represent a Listener’s Musical Taste?
text:
Results
Our listener likes First Light, Begin Again, and Morning Resolve. Their descriptions concern heartbreak, recovery, and starting over. The next cell prints the top three unheard songs using the centroid and cosine ranking, with the genre preference set to zero.

songs_by_id = {song.songId: song for song in songs}
listener = User(username="demo_listener")
for song_id in ("song_001", "song_002", "song_006"):
    listener.add_listen(songs_by_id[song_id])
recommender = SongRecommender(songs, collection)
recommendations = recommender.get_recommendations(
    listener.listening_history, same_genre_weight=0.0
)

print("Liked:")
for song in listener.listening_history.songs:
    print(f"  {song.title} ({song.genre})")
print("\nRecommended unheard songs:")
for rank, song in enumerate(recommendations, start=1):
    print(f"  {rank}. {song.title} ({song.genre}) — {song.songId}")
    print(f"     {song.description}")

Liked:
  First Light (Pop)
  Begin Again (Indie pop)
  Morning Resolve (Acoustic)

Recommended unheard songs:
  1. Last Letter (Folk) — song_008
     A bittersweet song about saying goodbye to a former partner and learning to let go.
  2. Beside You (Pop) — song_020
     A tender love song about trust and finding comfort in a lasting relationship.
  3. Empty Room (Pop) — song_007
     A slow ballad about loneliness and missing someone after a painful breakup.

title: Can Embeddings Represent a Listener’s Musical Taste?
text:
Analysis
Why did these songs rank highly? In the saved run, Last Letter ranks first and shares the themes of goodbye and letting go. Empty Room also concerns a breakup. Beside You is about comfort in a relationship, which is a looser textual connection. These are plausible readings of the descriptions, not a way to inspect exactly what the embedding model learned.
Why include genre? A song can have a similar description but belong to a different genre. As an optional preference, we count how many distinct liked songs have the candidate’s exact genre, then divide by the number of distinct liked songs. This gives a fraction from 0 to 1. Here the listener likes Pop, Indie pop, and Acoustic, so a Pop candidate gets 1/3; a Folk candidate gets 0. Pop and Indie pop are different labels.
With same_genre_weight=0, genre has no effect on the ranking. At 0.15, the score is 85% rescaled cosine similarity and 15% genre match. The comparison below shows how favoring a familiar genre can change the order; it cannot tell us whether the listener would enjoy the song.

for weight in (0.0, 0.15):
    titles = [
        song.title
        for song in recommender.get_recommendations(
            listener.listening_history, same_genre_weight=weight
        )
    ]
    print(f"Genre weight {weight:.2f}: {', '.join(titles)}")

Genre weight 0.00: Last Letter, Beside You, Empty Room
Genre weight 0.15: Beside You, Empty Room, Last Letter


In this run, the Pop genre match moves Beside You and Empty Room ahead of Last Letter. That is a design choice layered on the centroid experiment. Beside You is a love song rather than a song about getting over a breakup, so the new order is not automatically better.

title: Can Embeddings Represent a Listener’s Musical Taste?
text:
Failure cases
Text similarity is not musical preference. The model reads titles and descriptions, not audio. It cannot hear tempo, vocals, instrumentation, or production style, and a play is not necessarily a like. Averaging also loses detail when someone enjoys several different styles: one point in vector space may sit between them.
Try a second listener who likes quieter songs. The code still returns three unheard songs even if the catalog does not contain three strong matches. You can replace these song IDs with others from songs.csv to test a different history.

second_listener = User(username="quiet_listener")
for song_id in ("song_004", "song_005", "song_014"):
    second_listener.add_listen(songs_by_id[song_id])

print("Liked:", ", ".join(song.title for song in second_listener.listening_history.songs))
for song in recommender.get_recommendations(
    second_listener.listening_history, same_genre_weight=0.0
):
    print(f"Suggested: {song.title} ({song.genre}) — {song.description}")

Liked: Rain on the Window, Evening Drizzle, Quiet Pages
Suggested: Breathe Slowly (Ambient) — A peaceful instrumental track with flowing sounds for meditation and relaxation.
Suggested: Golden Afternoon (Dance pop) — A cheerful summer song about sunshine and dancing at an outdoor festival.
Suggested: Summer Pulse (Dance pop) — An energetic dance song for a summer party.


In the saved run, Breathe Slowly fits the quiet songs, while the dance tracks are surprising. This is a useful failure case: the method can fill the requested three slots without knowing whether the later results are good enough. A real recommender might require a minimum score and return fewer songs.

title: Can Embeddings Represent a Listener’s Musical Taste?
text:
Conclusion
Preference vectors work as a simple content-based baseline, but lose information. The centroid retrieves some thematically related, unheard songs from this small catalog. It compresses several interests into one vector, relies on song text rather than sound, and has not been evaluated against real listener preferences. These results support a limited claim about text retrieval, not a claim that we have captured musical taste.

title: Can Embeddings Represent a Listener’s Musical Taste?
text:
Where we’re going next
This notebook ends with a ranked list of unheard songs. To build on it, we can use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to explain those recommendations. We would give a language model the liked songs and the retrieved songs’ titles, genres, and descriptions, then ask it to explain why each recommendation fits. The catalog records provide the context for its answer.
The flow becomes: listening history → preference vector → Chroma search → ranked unheard songs → explanation based on their descriptions. We can then check whether each explanation points to evidence in the retrieved descriptions. The model still cannot tell from this text how a song sounds or whether the listener would enjoy it.

title: AI Engineering Lab
text: I use small, reproducible experiments to understand embeddings, search, and retrieval systems. Each notebook records the question, implementation, result, and next engineering decision.

title: AI Engineering Lab
text:
Embeddings and search

Text Embeddings and Semantic Search builds a song search engine and compares a keyword baseline with embedding retrieval.
A Content-Based Song Recommender uses three liked songs to recommend unheard songs and inspects the limits of text-based preference vectors.
Understanding RAG Through Song Recommendation Explanations shows how retrieval, context, and generation work together, where RAG is useful, and its limitations.

The source notebooks and song dataset are available in the repository.

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
text:
Imagine someone searches our song catalog for “A gentle track about losing a loved one and remembering them.” One description says, “A quiet song about grieving someone who has died and holding on to their memory.” The wording differs, but the theme is close. How can a search engine find it?
A basic keyword search checks whether query words appear in a song’s text. It is easy to understand and useful when words match. Semantic search instead compares representations of the query and songs, so it can retrieve related wording. I will build a small song search engine to test this difference, starting with what an embedding represents.

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
text:
Imagine someone searches our song catalog for “A gentle track about losing a loved one and remembering them.” One description says, “A quiet song about grieving someone who has died and holding on to their memory.” The wording differs, but the theme is close. How can a search engine find it?
A basic keyword search checks whether query words appear in a song’s text. It is easy to understand and useful when words match. Semantic search instead compares representations of the query and songs, so it can retrieve related wording. I will build a small song search engine to test this difference, starting with what an embedding represents.

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
text:
From text to vectors
An embedding is a vector of numbers produced by a model. For text retrieval, we encode a sentence or document as one vector and compare it with a query vector. The model has been trained so that related texts can have related representations. Similarity is useful evidence, not a guarantee that two texts mean the same thing.
There are two related uses of the word embedding:








Use
What is represented
What happens next




Token embeddings inside a language model
A token ID is mapped to a learned vector
The model processes it with context from other tokens.


Text embeddings for retrieval
A sentence, paragraph, or document is encoded as one vector
A search system compares it with query vectors.



This notebook uses the second kind. Both stored song text and search queries must pass through the same text embedding model.

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
text:
Our first text embedding
I use the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embedding model to encode three descriptions. It produces 384 numbers for each one. The next cell compares the first description with itself and the other two using cosine similarity.

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
sentences = [
    "A song about finding hope after heartbreak.",
    "An uplifting track about starting over after a breakup.",
    "An energetic dance song for a summer party.",
]
embeddings = model.encode(sentences)
similarities = model.similarity(embeddings[:1], embeddings)[0]

print(f"Dimensions: {embeddings.shape[1]}")
for sentence, score in zip(sentences, similarities):
    print(f"{score:.4f}  {sentence}")

Dimensions: 384
1.0000  A song about finding hope after heartbreak.
0.6546  An uplifting track about starting over after a breakup.
0.3642  An energetic dance song for a summer party.

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
section: Experiment: do similar meanings produce similar vectors?
text:
Experiment: do similar meanings produce similar vectors?
The model assigns the breakup descriptions a higher cosine similarity than the summer party description:



Comparison with “finding hope after heartbreak”
Cosine similarity




The same description
1.0000


Starting over after a breakup
0.6546


A summer party
0.3642



The first score is 1 because a vector is compared with itself. The second pair uses different words but shares a theme. This is one small example, not proof that the model will understand every paraphrase or that a particular score always means “relevant.”

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
text:
Before 384 dimensions, let’s understand three
The fruit example makes vector space easier to see. These coordinates are chosen by hand, not learned by an embedding model. Each vector has three coordinates in the order (sweetness, size, citrus intensity):



Fruit
Vector
Description




Banana
(8, 7, 0)
Very sweet, moderately large, non-citrus


Apple
(5, 6, 1)
Moderately sweet, medium-sized, slightly citrusy


Lemon
(2, 4, 8)
Not very sweet, smaller, strongly citrusy






Three-dimensional plot of banana, apple, lemon, and a query vector, with sweetness on the x-axis, size on the y-axis, and citrus intensity on the z-axis.


The plot places apple and banana relatively close together because both have higher sweetness and size values and low citrus intensity. Lemon lies farther toward the citrus axis. This shows how the chosen features position fruits in a vector space. Cosine similarity compares directions from the origin, rather than straight-line distances on the plot.
Here, the fruit vectors and query use the same three features. Real text embeddings use learned coordinates instead of hand-labeled features.

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
text:
Cosine similarity from scratch
For two nonzero vectors \(A\) and \(B\), the formula is:
\[
\cos(\theta) = \frac{A \cdot B}{\lVert A \rVert\,\lVert B \rVert}
\]
The dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds the results. The magnitudes in the denominator normalize vector length, so the score reflects direction. For the query \(Q=(6,6,2)\) and apple \(A=(5,6,1)\):

Dot product: \(Q\cdot A=6(5)+6(6)+2(1)=30+36+2=68\).
Magnitudes: \(\lVert Q \rVert=\sqrt{36+36+4}=\sqrt{76}\) and \(\lVert A \rVert=\sqrt{25+36+1}=\sqrt{62}\).
Similarity: \(68/(\sqrt{76}\sqrt{62})\approx0.9906\), displayed as 0.991 to three decimal places.

The next cell uses (6, 6, 2) as a query for a moderately sweet, medium-sized fruit with a little citrus and ranks the stored fruit vectors by cosine similarity.

from math import sqrt

fruits = {
    'Banana': (8, 7, 0),
    'Apple': (5, 6, 1),
    'Lemon': (2, 4, 8),
}
query = (6, 6, 2)

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    dot_product = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    magnitude_a = sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    magnitude_b = sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    return dot_product / (magnitude_a * magnitude_b)

ranked = sorted(
    ((fruit, cosine_similarity(query, vector)) for fruit, vector in fruits.items()),
    key=lambda result: result[1],
    reverse=True,
)

for fruit, score in ranked:
    print(f'{fruit}: {score:.3f}')

Apple: 0.991
Banana: 0.971
Lemon: 0.651


The query scores about 0.991 with apple, 0.971 with banana, and 0.651 with lemon, so apple ranks first. These scores compare vector directions, not absolute differences in individual fruit features.
These coordinates were chosen by hand to describe fruit. They cannot meaningfully describe Apple Inc., because sweetness, size, and citrus intensity are fruit attributes. Real text embeddings are learned from data and have many more dimensions; individual coordinates usually do not have simple, human-readable meanings.

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
text:
From three dimensions to 384
The fruit coordinates have labels we chose: sweetness, size, and citrus intensity. The MiniLM vectors have 384 learned coordinates. We should not label an individual coordinate “sadness” or “genre”: useful information is distributed across the vector, and individual numbers are generally hard to interpret on their own.
The comparison principle is the same in both examples: put the query and candidate items in the same space, then compare their vectors. The fruit code uses cosine similarity explicitly. The Chroma collection below uses its configured distance measure, which we have not set to cosine.

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
section: Building a semantic song search engine
text:
Building a semantic song search engine
The song dataset has 24 fictional songs. I combine each title and description into one text document. Chroma calls the same MiniLM model to embed those documents and keeps their IDs and other fields as metadata.
songs.csv → title + description → MiniLM embedding → Chroma collection
search text → MiniLM embedding → nearby song vectors → song metadata
The embedding model produces the representation; Chroma stores and searches it. The database’s distance calculation works on vectors and does not independently infer a song’s meaning. This example uses an in-memory Chroma client, so running the next cell rebuilds the collection for the current session. upsert lets the cell run again without duplicating IDs.

import chromadb
from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions
import pandas as pd

songs_df = pd.read_csv("songs.csv")
rows = songs_df.to_dict("records")

client = chromadb.Client()
embedding_function = embedding_functions.SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(
    model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
)
collection = client.get_or_create_collection(
    "song_search", embedding_function=embedding_function
)
collection.upsert(
    ids=[row["id"] for row in rows],
    documents=[f'{row["title"]} {row["description"]}' for row in rows],
    metadatas=[
        {
            "songId": row["id"],
            "title": row["title"],
            "genre": row["genre"],
            "description": row["description"],
        }
        for row in rows
    ],
)
print(f"Indexed {collection.count()} songs")

Indexed 24 songs



Searching songs by meaning
Now I query with wording that does not repeat the target song’s description. Chroma embeds the query with MiniLM and requests the three nearest songs. Results are grouped by input query, so results["metadatas"][0] selects the matches for this one query.

query = "A gentle track about losing a loved one and remembering them."
results = collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=3)

for rank, metadata in enumerate(results["metadatas"][0], start=1):
    print(f'{rank}. {metadata["title"]} ({metadata["genre"]}) — {metadata["songId"]}')
    print(f'   {metadata["description"]}')

1. Missing Your Voice (Piano ballad) — song_023
   A quiet song about grieving someone who has died and holding on to their memory.
2. Last Letter (Folk) — song_008
   A bittersweet song about saying goodbye to a former partner and learning to let go.
3. First Light (Pop) — song_001
   A song about finding hope after heartbreak.


The saved result ranks these songs for the paraphrased query:

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
section: Experiment: keyword search versus semantic search
text:
Experiment: keyword search versus semantic search
To make the comparison concrete, I use the same query and the same title plus description text for two approaches. The keyword baseline counts distinct query words appearing in each document after lowercasing and removing a small, explicitly listed set of common words. It is intentionally simple: it does not stem words, expand synonyms, or use a mature text search engine. The semantic ranking comes from the Chroma query above.
I report the top three matches from each approach and check how many selected query words appear in the target song.

import re

stop_words = {
    "a", "an", "the", "about", "and", "them", "one", "of", "to",
    "for", "with", "in", "on", "their", "someone",
}

def content_words(text):
    return set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text.lower())) - stop_words

query_words = content_words(query)
keyword_matches = []
for row in rows:
    song_text = f'{row["title"]} {row["description"]}'
    shared_words = query_words & content_words(song_text)
    if shared_words:
        keyword_matches.append((len(shared_words), row["id"], row["title"]))

keyword_matches.sort(key=lambda item: (-item[0], item[1]))
print(f"Query words checked: {', '.join(sorted(query_words))}")
print("Keyword top 3 (ties by song ID):")
for count, song_id, title in keyword_matches[:3]:
    print(f"  {song_id}: {title} ({count} matching word)")

print("Semantic top 3:")
for metadata in results["metadatas"][0]:
    print(f'  {metadata["songId"]}: {metadata["title"]}')

target = next(row for row in rows if row["id"] == "song_023")
target_text = f'{target["title"]} {target["description"]}'
print(f"Target keyword overlap: {len(query_words & content_words(target_text))}")

Query words checked: gentle, losing, loved, remembering, track
Keyword top 3 (ties by song ID):
  song_002: Begin Again (1 matching word)
  song_005: Evening Drizzle (1 matching word)
  song_009: City After Dark (1 matching word)
Semantic top 3:
  song_023: Missing Your Voice
  song_008: Last Letter
  song_001: First Light
Target keyword overlap: 0


The target has zero overlap with the selected query words, so this baseline does not return it. Chroma places it first. This demonstrates the value of embeddings for this paraphrase. It does not establish that semantic search always wins: lexical search can be better for exact titles, IDs, unusual names, or when an embedding model misses the intent. A larger evaluation would need labeled queries and relevance judgments.

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
text:
Scaling vector search
With 24 songs, comparing the query against every vector is practical. Exact k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) search computes distances for the stored candidates and returns the true nearest k under the chosen measure. Approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes can reduce search work in larger collections, sometimes at the cost of missing a true neighbor.
HNSW is one ANN method. It builds a graph of vector relationships and explores promising paths during retrieval. That introduces an engineering trade-off between latency, memory, and recall. Here, recall means the fraction of exact nearest neighbors found by the approximate search; it does not measure whether a song actually fits a listener’s request. We need a larger dataset and representative queries to measure that trade-off. No speed or recall benchmark is claimed for this 24-song example.

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
text:
What I learned
The fruit vectors made cosine similarity understandable, but their named coordinates are only an illustration. MiniLM’s 384 coordinates are learned and do not have simple labels. The song experiment showed me a more useful distinction: a small keyword baseline missed the grief song because the selected words were absent, while the embedding search ranked it first. It also showed why I must keep the model and the search system separate in my reasoning: MiniLM creates the vectors; Chroma retrieves nearby vectors. The next question is how retrieval quality and latency change when the collection grows.

title: Text Embeddings and Semantic Search
text:
Where I’m going next
Next, I’ll use a listener’s song history to build a simple content-based recommender. I’ll combine the embeddings of songs they liked into a preference vector, search the Chroma collection for similar songs they have not heard, and inspect where recommendations based only on titles and descriptions fall short. With 24 fictional songs, this will be a small demonstration rather than a performance benchmark.

title: Understanding RAG Through Song Recommendation Explanations
text:
The purpose of this notebook is to understand RAG, how it works, and where it is useful.
RAG stands for Retrieval Augmented Generation. It combines a search system with a language model: the search finds relevant information, and the language model uses that information to write an answer.
We use song recommendations as a small, concrete example. A recommender first chooses songs. We then collect relevant descriptions and lyrics and ask Llama to explain possible connections with the songs the listener likes.
By the end, you should be able to explain how source text becomes searchable, how retrieved passages become part of a prompt, and how to check an answer against its sources. You should also understand when RAG is useful and what it cannot guarantee.
The song recommender provides the example; recommendation itself is not a required part of RAG. The same retrieval and generation steps can answer questions about manuals, policies, research papers, and other document collections.

title: Understanding RAG Through Song Recommendation Explanations
text:
The purpose of this notebook is to understand RAG, how it works, and where it is useful.
RAG stands for Retrieval Augmented Generation. It combines a search system with a language model: the search finds relevant information, and the language model uses that information to write an answer.
We use song recommendations as a small, concrete example. A recommender first chooses songs. We then collect relevant descriptions and lyrics and ask Llama to explain possible connections with the songs the listener likes.
By the end, you should be able to explain how source text becomes searchable, how retrieved passages become part of a prompt, and how to check an answer against its sources. You should also understand when RAG is useful and what it cannot guarantee.
The song recommender provides the example; recommendation itself is not a required part of RAG. The same retrieval and generation steps can answer questions about manuals, policies, research papers, and other document collections.

title: Understanding RAG Through Song Recommendation Explanations
text:
2. What Is RAG?
Imagine asking an assistant a question about a document it has not been given. Its general knowledge may be insufficient or out of date. RAG addresses this by finding relevant source text and giving it to the model with the question.
There are two stages.
Prepare the information. Load documents, split them into smaller passages called chunks, and convert those chunks into embeddings. An embedding is a list of numbers that helps us compare text by meaning. Store the chunks, embeddings, and source details in a searchable collection.
Answer a request. Search for useful passages, put them in the prompt, and ask the language model to answer using them. This gives RAG its name:

Retrieval: Find relevant information.
Augmentation: Add that information to the model’s prompt.
Generation: Produce an answer using the supplied context.

For example, a question about returning a product could retrieve the relevant paragraph from a store’s return policy. The model can then explain the policy using that paragraph rather than guessing from general knowledge.
In this notebook, the request is to explain a song recommendation. We retrieve passages from the liked songs and the recommended song, add them to the prompt, and ask Llama to describe a supported connection. MiniLM creates embeddings, Chroma performs the search, and Llama writes the answer.
There are two searches here: one selects songs, while the other retrieves evidence for the explanation. Only the second search supplies the passages used in the RAG explanation. The selected songs are already fixed when Llama receives the prompt.
RAG does not retrain the language model. It provides information for the current answer. Updating the source collection can therefore change the evidence available to the model without changing its trained weights.

title: Understanding RAG Through Song Recommendation Explanations
text:
3. What Will We Compare?
To see the role of retrieved context, we ask Llama to explain each recommendation twice.
Without retrieved passages: Supply only the song IDs, titles, and genres.
With retrieved passages: Supply the same details plus relevant descriptions and lyrics.
We expect the supplied passages to make explanations more specific and easier to check. The comparison lets us inspect what changes when a model has source material available, rather than assuming RAG always improves an answer.
Each passage has a chunk ID so we can find its text and check the model’s claims. This demonstrates the contribution of context; it does not establish that searching is better than supplying the entire small catalog.

title: Understanding RAG Through Song Recommendation Explanations
text:
4. Experiment Setup
We use eight historical songs with public domain lyrics. This small catalog is separate from the fictional catalog in the earlier notebooks and makes the evidence easy to inspect.







Component
Role




public-domain-songs.csv
Song details, descriptions, source links, and rights notes


public-domain-song-lyrics.csv
Lyric sections linked to songs


all-MiniLM-L6-v2
Convert text into embeddings for search


Chroma
Store embeddings and find similar records


llama3.2:3b
Write explanations from the supplied records



The data contains text, not audio. Descriptions were written for this experiment; source links identify the historical lyrics. Modern recordings and arrangements may have separate rights.
Run Llama locally using Ollama. Download the model and keep Ollama running:
ollama pull llama3.2:3b
The next cell imports the libraries and sets the model and number of recommendations. We set temperature to 0 to reduce variation between answers, though this does not guarantee identical or correct output.

import csv
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

import chromadb
from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from ollama import Client

GENERATION_MODEL = "llama3.2:3b"
TEMPERATURE = 0
N_RECOMMENDATIONS = 3


Load the catalog
Read the CSV rows into Song and LyricSection objects. One song can have several lyric sections, connected by song_id.
The code checks that every lyric section belongs to an existing song. The path fallback allows execution from either the repository root or this notebook’s directory.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Song:
    song_id: str
    title: str
    artist: str
    genre: str
    description: str
    source_url: str
    rights_note: str

    def recommendation_text(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.title} {self.description}"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LyricSection:
    song_id: str
    section: str
    text: str


catalog_path = Path("public-domain-songs.csv")
lyrics_path = Path("public-domain-song-lyrics.csv")
if not catalog_path.exists():
    catalog_path = Path("embeddings-and-search") / catalog_path
    lyrics_path = Path("embeddings-and-search") / lyrics_path

with catalog_path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as song_file:
    songs = [
        Song(
            song_id=row["id"],
            title=row["title"],
            artist=row["artist"],
            genre=row["genre"],
            description=row["description"],
            source_url=row["source_url"],
            rights_note=row["rights_note"],
        )
        for row in csv.DictReader(song_file)
    ]


with lyrics_path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as lyrics_file:
    lyric_sections = [
        LyricSection(
            song_id=row["song_id"],
            section=row["section"],
            text=row["text"],
        )
        for row in csv.DictReader(lyrics_file)
    ]

songs_by_id = {song.song_id: song for song in songs}
unknown_lyric_ids = {section.song_id for section in lyric_sections} - songs_by_id.keys()
if unknown_lyric_ids:
    raise ValueError(f"Lyrics reference unknown songs: {sorted(unknown_lyric_ids)}")

print(f"Loaded {len(songs)} public-domain songs")
print(f"Loaded {len(lyric_sections)} lyric sections")

Loaded 8 public-domain songs
Loaded 27 lyric sections




Chunk the explanation evidence
A chunk is a short passage used as evidence. Searching passages helps us select relevant text and cite its exact source.
The splitter tries paragraph, line, sentence, and space boundaries. Here, chunk_size=180 limits chunks to about 180 characters, while chunk_overlap=30 allows nearby chunks to share about 30 characters to preserve context. Short descriptions and lyric sections can remain intact.
Larger chunks preserve more context; smaller chunks focus the search. Overlap can protect a phrase at a boundary but also repeats text. These settings are teaching examples, not universal defaults.
Each chunk keeps its song ID, source type, section, URL, and rights note.

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". " , " "],
    chunk_size=180,
    chunk_overlap=30,
)

description_sources = [
    {
        "song": song,
        "source_type": "description",
        "section": "catalog_description",
        "text": song.description,
    }
    for song in songs
]

lyric_sources = [
    {
        "song": songs_by_id[lyric.song_id],
        "source_type": "lyrics",
        "section": lyric.section,
        "text": lyric.text,
    }
    for lyric in lyric_sections
]

evidence_sources = description_sources + lyric_sources

evidence_chunks = []
for source in evidence_sources:
    song = source["song"]
    for chunk_index, text in enumerate(splitter.split_text(source["text"])):
        evidence_chunks.append(
            {
                "id": (
                    f"{song.song_id}:{source['source_type']}:"
                    f"{source['section']}:chunk-{chunk_index}"
                ),
                "text": text,
                "metadata": {
                    "song_id": song.song_id,
                    "title": song.title,
                    "genre": song.genre,
                    "source_type": source["source_type"],
                    "section": source["section"],
                    "source_url": song.source_url,
                    "rights_note": song.rights_note,
                    "chunk_index": chunk_index,
                },
            }
        )

print(f"Created {len(evidence_chunks)} evidence chunks from {len(evidence_sources)} sources")
for chunk in evidence_chunks[:3]:
    print(f"\n{chunk['id']}: {chunk['text']}")

Created 65 evidence chunks from 35 sources

pd_001:description:catalog_description:chunk-0: A song of longing for an absent loved one, remembered through images of summer, flowing water, and a voice that is gone.

pd_002:description:catalog_description:chunk-0: A declaration of lasting devotion to Annie Laurie, whose remembered promise inspires complete loyalty.

pd_003:description:catalog_description:chunk-0: A promise that love will endure after youth and beauty fade, grounded in constancy rather than appearance.




Build two indexes








Collection
Stores
Used for




Recommendation
One title and description document per song
Choosing similar songs


Evidence
Description and lyric chunks with source details
Gathering passages for explanations



Keeping these separate means songs with more lyrics do not get extra entries in the recommendation search. MiniLM embeds the text in both collections.
upsert inserts new IDs or updates existing IDs, so rerunning the cell does not duplicate those records.

client = chromadb.Client()
embedding_function = embedding_functions.SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(
    model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
)

recommendation_collection = client.get_or_create_collection(
    name="public_domain_song_recommendations",
    embedding_function=embedding_function,
    configuration={"hnsw": {"space": "cosine"}},
)
recommendation_collection.upsert(
    ids=[song.song_id for song in songs],
    documents=[song.recommendation_text() for song in songs],
)

evidence_collection = client.get_or_create_collection(
    name="public_domain_song_evidence",
    embedding_function=embedding_function,
    configuration={"hnsw": {"space": "cosine"}},
)
evidence_collection.upsert(
    ids=[chunk["id"] for chunk in evidence_chunks],
    documents=[chunk["text"] for chunk in evidence_chunks],
    metadatas=[chunk["metadata"] for chunk in evidence_chunks],
)

print(f"Indexed {recommendation_collection.count()} songs")
print(f"Indexed {evidence_collection.count()} evidence chunks")

title: Understanding RAG Through Song Recommendation Explanations
text:
5. Retrieval: Find Candidate Songs
Before explaining anything, we need songs to explain. recommend() retrieves the embeddings of the liked songs and averages them into one vector representing the listener’s interests. Chroma ranks catalog songs by similarity to that vector. The function excludes liked songs and returns the requested number of recommendations.
This is a comparison of text meanings, not a comparison of audio. An average can blur different interests, so it may return weak matches. Llama does not select or rerank the songs; the explanation stage should make a weak connection visible rather than disguise it.

def recommend(liked: list[Song], n_results: int = 3) -> list[Song]:
    liked_ids = list(dict.fromkeys(song.song_id for song in liked))
    if not liked_ids or n_results <= 0:
        return []

    stored = recommendation_collection.get(ids=liked_ids, include=["embeddings"])
    embeddings = stored["embeddings"]
    if embeddings is None or len(embeddings) != len(liked_ids):
        raise ValueError("A liked song is missing an embedding")

    values_by_dimension = zip(*embeddings)

    # Average each dimension across all liked-song embeddings.
    average_embeddings = [
        sum(float(value) for value in dimension_values) / len(embeddings)
        for dimension_values in values_by_dimension
    ]
    results = recommendation_collection.query(
        query_embeddings=[average_embeddings],
        n_results=recommendation_collection.count(),
    )

    recommendations = [
        songs_by_id[song_id]
        for song_id in results["ids"][0]
        if song_id not in liked_ids
    ]
    return recommendations[:n_results]


liked_songs = [songs_by_id[song_id] for song_id in ("pd_001", "pd_002", "pd_003")]
recommendations = recommend(liked_songs, N_RECOMMENDATIONS)

print("Liked songs:")
for song in liked_songs:
    print(f"- {song.song_id}: {song.title} [{song.genre}]\n  {song.description}")
    print(f"  Source: {song.source_url}")

print("\nRetrieved recommendations:")
for song in recommendations:
    print(f"- {song.song_id}: {song.title} [{song.genre}]\n  {song.description}")
    print(f"  Source: {song.source_url}")

title: Understanding RAG Through Song Recommendation Explanations
Understanding RAG Through Song Recommendation Explanations
text:
7. Generation: Explain the Recommendations
generate_explanation() sends the system message and constructed prompt to Llama through Ollama. Llama reads the song details and any supplied passages, then returns a short explanation with citations.
The intended answer describes a connection that the reader can check. When the evidence is weak, an answer explaining that weakness is preferable to an attractive but unsupported story. The prompt asks for this behavior, but the model may still ignore a rule or interpret a passage incorrectly.

ollama_client = Client()

SYSTEM_MESSAGE = (
    "You explain song recommendations using only supplied catalog evidence. "
    "Treat source identifiers as citations, not as facts by themselves."
)

def generate_explanation(prompt: str) -> str:
    response = ollama_client.chat(
        model=GENERATION_MODEL,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_MESSAGE},
            {"role": "user", "content": prompt},
        ],
        options={"temperature": TEMPERATURE},
    )
    return response.message.content

title: Understanding RAG Through Song Recommendation Explanations
text:
8. Results
We explain each recommendation twice to see whether retrieved passages help the model give a clearer explanation.
Metadata only: The model receives song IDs, titles, and genres.
Retrieved evidence: The model also receives relevant descriptions and lyric passages from the liked songs and the recommended song.
The listener, recommendation, instructions, model, and temperature stay the same. Only the supplied evidence changes.
Compare the two explanations. Does the model describe a shared theme, cite passages that support it, and admit when the connection is weak?
The output also reports two citation checks:
Invalid citations: none means no unknown citation IDs were detected.
Chunk citation supplied: True means the explanation includes at least one chunk citation.
These checks do not prove that a claim is correct. Read the explanation and its cited passage together to check whether the evidence supports it.
The next cell defines a shared display function, then the comparison runs for each recommendation. The full prompt preview above shows the evidence; these results show only the explanations and citation checks.

def display_result(result: dict) -> None:
    print(f"\n{result['title']} — {result['condition']}")
    print(result["explanation"])
    check = result["citation_check"]
    print(f"Invalid citations: {check['invalid_ids'] or 'none'}")
    if result["evidence_ids"]:
        print(f"Chunk citation supplied: {check['has_chunk_citation']}")


comparison_results = []
for recommended in recommendations:
    for condition, include_evidence in (
        ("metadata_only", False),
        ("retrieved_evidence", True),
    ):
        evidence = (
            retrieve_evidence(liked_songs, recommended)
            if include_evidence
            else None
        )
        context = build_context(liked_songs, recommended, evidence=evidence)
        explanation = generate_explanation(build_prompt(context, recommended))
        citation_check = check_citations(
            explanation, liked_songs, recommended, evidence
        )
        comparison_results.append(
            {
                "song_id": recommended.song_id,
                "title": recommended.title,
                "condition": condition,
                "explanation": explanation,
                "evidence_ids": [
                    record["chunk_id"] for record in (evidence or [])
                ],
                "citation_check": citation_check,
            }
        )

for result in comparison_results:
    display_result(result)

title: Understanding RAG Through Song Recommendation Explanations
text:
9. Benefits, Drawbacks, and Failure Cases
The main benefit of explanation RAG is traceability: the reader can inspect the passages behind an explanation instead of accepting a general statement about the songs. It also lets the model use the catalog’s chosen text without relying on whether it encountered those sources during training.
That benefit depends on several things going right:







Limitation
What can happen here




Missing context
Two chunks per song can leave out a verse that changes the interpretation.


Weak retrieval
A search returns the closest passages even when none provides a strong connection.


Selective evidence
A query built from the recommendation can favor matching themes and miss contradictions.


Model mistakes
Llama can misread a passage, invent a detail, or attach a valid citation to an unsupported claim.


Extra work
Chunking, embeddings, searches, and longer prompts add complexity and runtime.


Limited scope
Lyrics and descriptions cannot establish audio qualities or whether the listener will enjoy a recording.



The lyric passages were not used to rank the recommendations, so they may support a plausible connection without explaining why the embedding search ranked a particular song highly.
Use this checklist to evaluate the answers:







Check
Question




Specificity
Does the explanation identify a clear shared or conflicting theme?


Citation validity
Were the cited IDs supplied in the prompt?


Support
Do the actual passages support the claims and quotations?


Caution
Does it admit weak connections and avoid promising enjoyment?



The next cell tries a listener with different interests. This explores less obvious connections, though it does not guarantee weak matches. The first recommendation is simply the closest available candidate, not necessarily a strong choice.
To audit a result, locate its chunk IDs in evidence_chunks and compare the text with each claim. Check evidence for both the liked songs and the recommended song. A fluent answer with valid IDs can still fail this review.

mixed_likes = [songs_by_id[song_id] for song_id in ("pd_005", "pd_008")]
mixed_recommendations = recommend(mixed_likes, N_RECOMMENDATIONS)

print("Mixed listener recommendations:")
for recommended in mixed_recommendations:
    print(f"- {recommended.song_id}: {recommended.title} — {recommended.description}")

for recommended in mixed_recommendations:
    evidence = retrieve_evidence(mixed_likes, recommended)
    context = build_context(mixed_likes, recommended, evidence=evidence)
    explanation = generate_explanation(build_prompt(context, recommended))
    display_result(
        {
            "title": recommended.title,
            "condition": "retrieved_evidence",
            "explanation": explanation,
            "evidence_ids": [record["chunk_id"] for record in evidence],
            "citation_check": check_citations(
                explanation, mixed_likes, recommended, evidence
            ),
        }
    )

title: Understanding RAG Through Song Recommendation Explanations
text:
10. Where Can We Apply RAG?
The song example demonstrates a reusable process: prepare a collection of source passages, retrieve the passages relevant to a request, add them to a prompt, and generate an answer. In another application, the documents and questions change, but these stages remain.








Application
What retrieval finds
What the model generates




Internal knowledge assistant
Relevant policies and team documentation
An answer based on the organization’s documents


Customer support
Product manuals and support articles
Instructions suited to the customer’s question


Research assistant
Relevant passages from selected papers
A summary or comparison with source references


Technical documentation assistant
Documentation for a particular product version
An explanation based on that version


Recommendation explanation
Descriptions and passages for selected items
An explanation of a possible connection



RAG is useful when answers depend on a document collection that is large, changes over time, or contains information the model may not know. Retrieval selects a manageable amount of source text for each request. Source IDs also give readers a way to inspect the evidence, although the application must preserve those references.
RAG adds work: sources must be prepared and maintained, retrieval takes time, and longer prompts add processing cost. A search can miss an important passage, and the model can misinterpret what it receives. In systems with private documents, retrieval must also respect which documents the user is allowed to access.
For a short document or this tiny song catalog, placing all relevant text directly in the prompt may be simpler. A direct database query is often better for an exact count or lookup. A task based only on general knowledge or creative writing may not need an external collection at all.
The central lesson is that retrieval supplies information, augmentation makes it available to the model, and generation turns it into an answer. Useful RAG requires both relevant sources and an answer that uses them accurately.

Next Step: From Supplying Evidence to Learning a Task
In this notebook, we supplied Llama with relevant passages so it could explain a recommendation. We changed the information available in its prompt without changing the model itself.
Now imagine this system receiving messages from users. Some ask for recommendations, others want an explanation, and others report a missing playlist. Before retrieving evidence or writing an answer, the application needs to decide what each message is asking for.
This introduces a new task: classifying intent using categories defined for our music service. A message such as “Why does this song keep appearing?” might ask for a recommendation explanation or report a playback problem. Correct routing depends on the context and the category rules we define. More song lyrics alone will not resolve that distinction.
We will first try clear instructions and labelled examples in the prompt. If the model repeatedly confuses our categories, we can investigate fine tuning: additional training on examples of messages and their expected labels. Unlike supplying passages through RAG, fine tuning updates the model’s trained parameters to encourage the desired classification behavior.








Example message
Category
Route




I like these songs. What else should I try?
Recommendation Request
Existing recommender, given liked song IDs


Why did you recommend this song?
Explanation Request
Existing RAG workflow, given the liked songs and recommendation


My playlist disappeared.
Customer Support
Support queue


Can we add our catalog to your service?
Partnership
Partnership queue


Buy followers through this link.
Junk
Junk queue


I have something to discuss.
Human Review
Human review queue



Start with sample messages rather than a live inbox. Classification identifies intent; the application must separately obtain the song IDs and other details needed to handle the request. Searching directly from a free text theme would require an additional recommendation search function.
In the next notebook, define the category rules and build a labelled dataset, including ambiguous messages that should go to human review. Establish a baseline using prompting, then fine tune on the training examples. Compare both approaches on the same unseen test messages, keeping those messages out of training and prompt examples.
The learning question is: Does fine tuning classify our messages more reliably than prompting alone? Examine mistakes by category, especially useful messages incorrectly marked as junk, and whether unclear messages reach human review. Fine tuning adds data preparation and training work, so the comparison should establish whether it is worthwhile.
Fine tuning therefore extends this application rather than replacing RAG. The classifier learns how to route messages according to our examples and rules. When a message requests a recommendation explanation, the existing RAG workflow still retrieves the source passages needed to answer it.
